slides.title: Magnetic confinement: requirements + dimensionless figures of merit
slides.body:
**The goal**: confine a 10-100 keV fully-ionized DT plasma at n ~ 10²⁰ m⁻³ long enough that fusion reactions release more energy than needed to heat + maintain it. Magnetic field is the only practical way to insulate a 100 million °C plasma from material walls — gyromotion across B is suppressed → χ_⊥ ~ ρ_L² ν ≪ χ_∥.

**Why toroidal?** Straight field lines would let particles stream out the ends. Wrapping field lines into a torus eliminates open ends. But a purely toroidal field is unstable: grad-B + curvature drifts separate charges → vertical E → outward E×B drift → loss. Solution: add a **poloidal field** so field lines twist → **rotational transform** ι = poloidal/toroidal winding → short-circuits charge separation.

**Key dimensionless parameters**:
- **Plasma β = p_thermal/p_magnetic = 2μ₀p/B²** — efficiency of using B-field. Tokamaks ~1-5%; spherical tokamaks (MAST-U, ST40) ~30-40%; reversed-field pinch ~10%; ICF compressed → β > 1. **Troyon limit**: β_max[%] ≈ 2.8 × I_p[MA]/(a[m] B[T]).
- **Safety factor q = (r B_φ)/(R B_θ)** = field-line winding number; q > 1 at center prevents kink instability; q(a)>2 avoids external kinks; **Kruskal-Shafranov limit** q > 1.
- **Greenwald density limit** n_GW[10²⁰ m⁻³] = I_p[MA]/(π a²[m²]) — empirical; exceeding it triggers MARFEs + disruptions.
- **Energy confinement time τ_E = W/P_loss** — central figure of merit; **IPB98(y,2) scaling** for H-mode (ITER design basis).
- **Bootstrap fraction f_BS = I_BS/I_p** — pressure-driven non-inductive current; reaches ~70-90% in advanced scenarios.
- **Pedestal pressure** — H-mode edge transport barrier; sets core performance via stiff profile constraint.

**Configurations**:
- **Tokamak** (T-3 1968 Artsimovich): axisymmetric, externally-driven toroidal current generates B_pol → simple but pulsed unless current driven non-inductively. Workhorse of fusion (JET, JT-60SA, EAST, KSTAR, DIII-D, ASDEX-U, NSTX-U, MAST-U, ST40, ITER, SPARC).
- **Stellarator**: 3D twisted coils generate full field externally — steady-state, no current-driven instabilities, but engineering complexity high. **W7-X** (Greifswald 2015–) is the optimized flagship.
- **Reversed-Field Pinch (RFP)**: high β, self-organized (Taylor relaxation); RFX-mod, MST.
- **Spheromak + FRC**: compact toroids, plasma-generated field — TAE Technologies, Helion.
- **Z-pinch + sheared-flow Z-pinch**: Zap Energy, ZaP.
- **Magnetic mirror**: open ends, leaky; revived in axisymmetric variants (Realta, Open Plasma).

slides.title: Tokamaks, stellarators, alternatives: a tour of fusion machines
slides.body:
**Tokamak** (тороидальная камера с магнитными катушками = 'toroidal chamber with magnetic coils', Soviet acronym):
- **T-3** (Kurchatov Institute, **Lev Artsimovich 1968**) — first to demonstrate T_e ~1 keV, blew away open competitors; confirmed by British Culham team with Thomson scattering → world adopted tokamak.
- **TFTR** (Princeton 1982-1997): first DT plasma 1993; 10.7 MW peak fusion (1994), Q ~ 0.27.
- **JET** (Joint European Torus, Culham, 1983–2023): JET DTE1 1997: 16 MW, Q = 0.67; **JET DTE2 2022: 59 MJ in 5 s** — record fusion energy in any machine.
- **JT-60U / JT-60SA** (Japan, JAEA): set Q_eq = 1.25 D-D equivalent; JT-60SA (2023 first plasma) is largest pre-ITER tokamak.
- **KSTAR** (Korea, 2008–): superconducting, all-Nb₃Sn coils, > 100 s H-mode 100 MK.
- **EAST** (China, 2006–): superconducting, ~1000 s LH-driven plasma.
- **DIII-D** (General Atomics): physics workhorse, negative-triangularity research.
- **ASDEX-Upgrade** (Garching): tungsten wall, ELM control benchmark.
- **NSTX-U / MAST-U / ST40**: spherical tokamaks (A=R/a ~ 1.5) — high β, compact.
- **ITER** (Cadarache, France, **first plasma 2034 (delayed); DT 2039**): R=6.2 m, B=5.3 T, I_p=15 MA, target **Q=10, 500 MW for 400 s**.
- **SPARC** (Commonwealth Fusion Systems / MIT, Devens MA, **first plasma 2027 target**): R=1.85 m, B=12.2 T REBCO HTS coils, target **Q≈11**.

**Stellarator** (Lyman Spitzer, Princeton 1951 — coined the term + invented the concept):
- **Wendelstein 7-X (W7-X)** (Greifswald, 2015–): optimized HELIAS, 50 superconducting non-planar coils, demonstrated steady-state low-turbulence operation; T_i ~ 3 keV at n ~ 10²⁰ m⁻³, 30 min plasmas; quasi-isodynamic optimization → minimal neoclassical transport.
- **LHD** (Toki, Japan, 1998–): largest stellarator; heliotron design.
- **TJ-II, HSX**: smaller research stellarators.
- **Type One Energy** (US private): stellarator startup using TAE / W7-X concepts.
- **Renaissance Fusion, Proxima** (EU): private stellarator efforts.

**Alternatives + private fusion**:
- **Commonwealth Fusion Systems (SPARC, ARC)**: HTS tokamak.
- **TAE Technologies**: FRC + neutral-beam stabilized (advanced fuels p-B11).
- **Helion Energy (Polaris)**: FRC + pulsed direct conversion (D-³He).
- **Zap Energy**: sheared-flow Z-pinch.
- **Tokamak Energy (ST40)**: compact spherical tokamak with HTS.
- **Realta, Avalanche, Marvel, Pacific Fusion, Xcimer**: ICF-like + hybrid.
- **Focused Energy** (US/Germany): direct-drive laser fusion.
- **First Light Fusion**: projectile-driven inertial fusion (acquired 2024).

**Why so many concepts now?** HTS breakthrough (~2020 commercial REBCO at 20 T-class fields), 2022 NIF ignition, climate urgency, private capital ($7B+ since 2020 per FIA).

slides.title: Lawson criterion + triple product + the road to ignition
slides.body:
**Lawson criterion** (John D. Lawson, AEA Harwell, **1955 internal report; 1957 Proc. Phys. Soc.**): for a fusion power plant to produce net energy, the energy released by fusion must exceed energy lost. For **DT fusion** with bremsstrahlung + transport losses:

$$n \tau_E \gtrsim \frac{12 T}{\langle\sigma v\rangle E_{ch}}$$

where E_ch = 3.5 MeV (alpha energy retained for self-heating); ⟨σv⟩ is fusion reactivity. For **DT ignition** the threshold is approximately:

$$n \tau_E \gtrsim 1.5 \times 10^{20} \text{ s/m}^3 \quad (\text{at } T = 15 \text{ keV})$$

**Triple product** (more useful figure of merit because reactivity peaks at finite T):

$$n T \tau_E \gtrsim 3 \times 10^{21} \text{ keV·s/m}^3 \quad (\text{at } T \approx 15 \text{ keV, the DT minimum})$$

The triple product has a **minimum at T ≈ 15 keV** for DT — colder plasma has low reactivity, hotter plasma loses too much to bremsstrahlung (∝ T^{1/2}) + transport. The **D-³He triple product threshold is ~10× higher** because no neutron heating + higher T optimum (~50 keV); **p-¹¹B is ~100× harder** still (TAE's pursuit).

**Q = P_fusion/P_aux** is the **fusion gain**:
- Q = 1 = **scientific breakeven**: fusion power equals injected heating.
- Q ≈ 5: **alpha heating dominant** over external (alpha is 20% of fusion energy; equilibrium when α-heating matches losses).
- **Q = ∞ = ignition**: alpha heating fully sustains plasma without external heating.
- Q ≈ 30-40: typical **economic / engineering breakeven** target for power plants (accounting for plant electricity, BOP, tritium breeding).

**Historical milestones**:
- **TFTR 1994**: 10.7 MW peak fusion, Q ≈ 0.27 (Princeton).
- **JET DTE1 1997**: 16 MW peak (5 s), 22 MJ total, Q = 0.67 (then-record).
- **JT-60U 1998**: Q_DD-equivalent ≈ 1.25 (would have been DT Q ≈ 1.25; no DT campaign).
- **JET DTE2 2022**: **59 MJ in 5 s** sustained — record fusion energy magnetic confinement.
- **NIF Dec 5 2022**: first laboratory ignition (Q_target = 3.15 MJ / 2.05 MJ = 1.54 — but inertial confinement, see next lesson).
- **ITER**: design target **Q=10, 500 MW for 400 s**; first plasma 2034 (delayed); DT 2039.
- **SPARC**: target **Q ≈ 11** in compact REBCO-HTS device; first plasma ~2027.
- **STEP** (UK Spherical Tokamak for Energy Production): operational 2040s target.
- **CFETR** (China Fusion Engineering Test Reactor): operational ~2035 target.

**Power-plant scaling**: ITER → DEMO (~2050) → first-of-a-kind power plant (~2060s public path; CFS/Helion private timelines 2030s). Key gating issues: **tritium breeding** (Li blanket modules, TBR > 1.1), **first-wall materials** (W, RAFM steels, neutron damage at 20-150 dpa), **disruption mitigation**, **divertor heat handling** (~10 MW/m² steady, much higher transient), **non-inductive current drive for steady-state**.

**Alpha self-heating significance**: NIF 2022 ignition demonstrated **alpha-particle self-heating > external drive** for the first time in lab — a watershed for the entire field. JET, ITER, SPARC chase the magnetic-confinement counterpart.

question.question: Apply triple product to assess SPARC vs ITER
question.goal: Estimate triple product n T τ_E for ITER (n=10²⁰, T=15 keV, τ_E=3.7 s) + SPARC (n=4×10²⁰, T=12 keV, τ_E=0.5 s); compare to Lawson.

steps.prompt: Compute n T τ_E for ITER.
steps.reveal: n T τ_E = 10²⁰ × 15 × 3.7 = **5.6×10²¹ keV·s/m³** — comfortably exceeds Lawson ~3×10²¹, consistent with Q=10.
n T τ_E = 4×10²⁰ × 12 × 0.5 = **2.4×10²¹ keV·s/m³** — just below Lawson, but with B=12.2 T → Greenwald limit relaxed, β-margin large → projected Q ≈ 11 in burning-plasma regime.

steps.prompt: Why does high B help compact reactors per τ_E ∝ B^α scaling?

acceptedAnswers: fusion power ~ β² B⁴ at fixed β; HTS gives 2× B → 16× power density

hints: P_fus/V ~ n² ⟨σv⟩ ~ (β B²)² × T²-like → ~ β² B⁴ for fixed T.
steps.reveal: At fixed β: p = β B²/(2μ_0) → n ∝ B² (at fixed T); P_fus/V ~ n²⟨σv⟩ ~ β² B⁴. Doubling B → 16× power density. **HTS REBCO** lets compact CFS-SPARC reach ITER-class Q in fraction of volume + cost. Also IPB98(y,2) gives τ_E ∝ B^0.15 I_p^0.93 → high I_p limited by Greenwald, but high B lets you push n proportionally.

steps.prompt: What's the alpha-heating self-sufficiency condition + when does ignition occur?

acceptedAnswers: P_α ≥ P_loss → ignition; for DT alpha = 20% of fusion = 0.2 P_fus → Q → ∞

hints: Alpha carries 3.5 MeV / (3.5+14.1 MeV) ≈ 20% of fusion energy.
steps.reveal: DT releases 17.6 MeV/reaction: 14.1 MeV to neutron (escapes plasma, breeds tritium in blanket), 3.5 MeV to alpha (stays + heats). **Ignition** = P_α ≥ P_loss → external heating not needed (Q → ∞). **Burning plasma** = alpha-heating dominant (Q ≳ 5). ITER aims Q=10 → alpha heating 5× external; SPARC Q≈11 similar. Sustaining ignition requires controllable α-channeling + avoiding burn instabilities.

question.question: Why is the **triple product n T τ_E** the canonical figure of merit instead of just n τ_E?
options: Fusion reactivity ⟨σv⟩(T) is a strong function of T — it rises steeply, peaks (DT at ~70 keV, broad), but **bremsstrahlung losses scale as √T** + thermal energy as T, so the **most efficient operating temperature is finite** (~15 keV for DT, ~50 keV for D-³He). The Lawson criterion n τ_E ≥ f(T) gives different thresholds at every T; the **triple product nTτ_E** absorbs the T-dependence into a quantity with a **clear minimum** at the optimal T → a single ~3×10²¹ keV·s/m³ target for DT. Useful because: (i) progress across machines + decades is benchmarked on one axis; (ii) trade-offs between n, T, τ_E (set by ∇p MHD limits, β limits, Greenwald limit, IPB98 scaling) are explicit; (iii) makes physics-engineering comparison (ITER, SPARC, JET, NIF, W7-X) commensurate. Recent rapid progress in private fusion + NIF ignition + JET 59 MJ are all benchmarked against triple-product targets.
question.explanation: Triple product n T τ_E captures the T-dependence of ⟨σv⟩ + bremsstrahlung losses → has a minimum at the optimal T (~15 keV DT). Lets us compare progress across machines/decades on a single axis. Standard target for DT: ~3×10²¹ keV·s/m³. Captures trade-offs in n, T, τ_E set by β limits + Greenwald limit + scaling laws.

hints: Why does the Lawson threshold depend on T?
slides.workedSolution: Reactivity ⟨σv⟩(T) rises + peaks; bremsstrahlung ∝ √T + thermal energy ∝ T means there's an optimal T (DT ~15 keV). The triple product n T τ_E is constructed so its threshold has a minimum at that optimal T (~3×10²¹ keV·s/m³ for DT), giving a single number that captures all the trade-offs. Standard benchmark across machines + decades; NIF 2022, JET 2022, ITER, SPARC all measured against it.

question.question: Why HTS changes the fusion landscape
question.prompt: Commonwealth Fusion Systems (SPARC) + Tokamak Energy bet on REBCO HTS coils at B = 12-20 T vs ITER's LTS Nb₃Sn at 5.3 T. Discuss (a) why P_fus/V ~ β² B⁴ matters for compact machines, (b) cost-scaling of magnets vs B, (c) engineering challenges of HTS at 20 T (Lorentz stress, joints, quench protection, neutron damage), (d) why this enabled the post-2020 private-fusion boom (>$7B raised since 2020).

question.question: Write the DT triple-product Lawson target at T=15 keV.
question.hint: Density × temperature × confinement time threshold for DT ignition.

question.prompt: In ≤120 words, explain how Lawson's 1957 criterion + the triple product set the bar for fusion + how today's machines (JET, ITER, SPARC, W7-X) compare.
question.rubric: Mentions: Lawson (1955/1957) — for net fusion energy need n τ_E ≥ ~10²⁰ s/m³; better is **triple product n T τ_E ≥ ~3×10²¹ keV·s/m³** for DT at optimal T~15 keV (minimum of T-dependent threshold). Defines **Q = P_fus/P_aux** (Q=1 breakeven, Q=∞ ignition). Tokamak progress: TFTR 1994 Q~0.27; JET DTE1 1997 Q=0.67; JET DTE2 2022 59 MJ — record; ITER targets Q=10, 500 MW; SPARC Q≈11 in compact HTS. Stellarator W7-X demonstrates steady-state low-turbulence regimes. P_fus/V ~ β² B⁴ rationale for HTS path. Concludes: Lawson stays the central benchmark; HTS + 2022 NIF ignition + JET 59 MJ unlocked the modern private-fusion era + put real engineering reactors within sight.
